title: South Asians Face Higher Heart Risk by 45 Despite Healthier Habits, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A decade-long Northwestern study of 2,700 adults reveals a troubling paradox: South Asians report better diets and lower alcohol use but develop prediabetes and hypertension at double the rate of white Americans by midlife.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • South Asians develop heart disease risk factors despite healthier diets and lower alcohol consumption.
  • By age 45, 31% of South Asian men have prediabetes, compared to 4% of white men.
  • A quarter of South Asian men have high blood pressure by age 45, exceeding other groups.
  • South Asians account for 60% of global heart disease patients, despite being 25% of the population.
  • Culturally tailored health screenings are crucial for South Asian adults to assess their risk.

Source: Journal of the American Heart Association
They eat well. They drink less. They exercise as much as everyone else. And yet, South Asian Americans are developing heart disease risk factors at rates that leave researchers searching for answers. A landmark study led by Northwestern Medicine, published in the *Journal of the American Heart Association*, followed 2,700 adults across a decade and uncovered what researchers are calling the South Asian cardiovascular paradox. Despite reporting healthier diets, lower alcohol consumption, and comparable physical activity levels, participants with heritage from India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka showed significantly higher rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension than nearly every other population group in the United States. ## The Numbers Are Stark At age 45, South Asian men had a prediabetes prevalence of 31 percent — compared to just 4 percent among white men, 10 percent among Black and Hispanic men, and 13 percent among Chinese men. South Asian women weren't far behind: nearly one in five had prediabetes by 45, roughly double the rate seen in women of other backgrounds. By age 55, both South Asian men and women were at least twice as likely to have developed full diabetes as their white counterparts. Hypertension rates told a similar story. At 45, a quarter of South Asian men had high blood pressure, exceeding rates among white, Hispanic, and Chinese men. High cholesterol and triglyceride levels were also elevated. > **""The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviors and clinical risk was surprising," said Dr."** "The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviors and clinical risk was surprising," said Dr. Namratha Kandula, professor of general internal medicine and epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and the study's senior author. "This paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians." ## Hidden Fat, Hidden Risk The study drew on data from two long-running cohorts: MASALA, which focuses specifically on South Asian adults in the United States, and MESA, which includes white, Black, Hispanic, and Chinese adults. By combining these datasets, researchers could directly compare how risk factors evolve across racial and ethnic groups during the same life stage. One critical clue lies beneath the skin. Prior research from the MASALA study has shown that South Asians tend to carry more visceral fat — fat deposited around internal organs — than other groups, even at a normal or low BMI. This pattern of hidden fat distribution begins in childhood and is a well-established driver of insulin resistance, inflammation, and cardiovascular disease. "Early life nutrition, environment, stressors, and activity patterns in childhood may increase cardiometabolic risks that show up by age 45," Kandula explained. Most MASALA participants are immigrants whose formative years were shaped by conditions in South Asia, potentially priming metabolic pathways that current lifestyle habits alone cannot reverse. ## A Global Burden The findings fit into a larger, alarming picture. Globally, South Asians make up roughly one-quarter of the world's population but account for an estimated 60 percent of heart disease patients worldwide. In the United States, where they are among the fastest-growing demographic groups, South Asians develop atherosclerosis — the hardening and narrowing of arteries that leads to heart attacks — up to a decade earlier than the general population. Standard clinical guidelines, however, still rely heavily on BMI thresholds and lifestyle questionnaires that were developed primarily in European populations. For South Asians, these tools may provide a dangerously incomplete picture of actual risk.

## What the Diaspora Needs to Know Kandula's message to South Asian patients is blunt: "Even if you eat well and exercise, you may still be at higher risk for diabetes and high blood pressure at younger ages." She recommends that South Asian adults ask their doctors about early screening — specifically, getting blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a) checked before middle age. Lipoprotein(a), a genetically determined risk factor that is elevated in many South Asians, is not part of standard cholesterol panels but can significantly improve risk assessment. For clinicians, the study underscores the need for culturally appropriate lifestyle counseling that goes beyond generic dietary advice. Understanding the carbohydrate-heavy diets common in South Asian households, the role of ghee and cooking oils, and the cultural barriers to discussing metabolic health are essential for effective intervention. Chandrika Gopal, a 58-year-old MASALA participant from Ohio, put it plainly: "Even if we eat well, we can still be at higher risk. Living in a new country, adapting to different food and routines — it all adds up." The study's authors say the window for prevention is narrow but real. The 40s represent a critical decade when risk is already high but disease is still preventable. For the 5.4 million South Asians living in the United States, that window is worth knowing about. *Sources: Journal of the American Heart Association (2026); Northwestern University News; MASALA Study (masalastudy.org); UCSF South Asian Heart Center*
